initial_response.topic: Well Test Analysis에서 interference testing은 두 우물 사이의 어떤 저류층 성질을 조사하는 용도로 설명되는가?
initial_response.goal: Well Test Analysis에서 interference testing은 두 우물 사이의 어떤 저류층 성질을 조사하는 용도로 설명되는가?
initial_response.final_answer:
Interference testing is used to investigate the transmissibility of the reservoir between two wells. [KB2] [KB3]
Interference testing helps determine the hydraulic connectivity between two wells in a reservoir. [KB2] [KB3]
Interference testing provides evidence of the presence of a continuous and permeable reservoir layer between two wells. [KB2] [KB3]

4.1 INTRODUCTION TO FAULT DETECTION
One of the most important tasks in the elucidation of reservoir structure is the 
identification of any linear sealing faults of the type illustrated diagrammatically in 
Figure 1.  This is of particular concern where recovery by displacement is envisaged 
and knowledge of the continuity between wells is essential.  The first evidence 
of the existence of faulting is usually obtained when recognisable zones show a 
displacement in depth between two wells after allowing for formation inclination; 
obviously the dip-meter is the key log in this exercise.  Single well testing may be 
able to confirm the presence of a linear boundary. However, in order to determine 
whether a fault is completely sealing or exhibits partial communication, it may be 
necessary to carry out interference tests.  The effect of a linear no-flow boundary 
on the pressure response observed at an active well must be analysed so that the 
process of fault detection can be understood and so that a well test can be properly 
interpreted for kh and skin even w

aviour.
However, once the field is on substantial production, transient pressure tests will 
be carried out both in new development wells as they are drilled and in existing 
producers or injectors which have been flowing for a considerable period.  The 
objective of this testing is to determine the well skin factors and to identify by 
inference the reservoir structure between the wells.  In the case of new development 
wells the local reservoir pressure, prior to flow, will usually be declining as a result 
of production from existing wells unless water injection has stabilised the system.  If 
there is no water influx the reservoir may well be in semi-steady-state depletion with 
the pressure decreasing linearly with time.  It is essential to determine by means of 
distributed pressure surveys whether substantial potential differences between layers 
have developed as a result of differential depletion.  If this has occurred a test on 
the new well will be influenced by crossflow through the wellbore during the shut-in 
period and proper analysis of the test will require a layered single well model.  In 
addition the test design should include flowmeter surveys both during the f

ation. The reason for determining an average permeability 
is in rationalising the permeability measured on small samples in the laboratory with 
the measurements made for example by well test analysis. Well test analysis can-
not test small sections of the reservoir (which would be uneconomical) on the same 
scale as the laboratory tests. The results are therefore representative of flow through 
several layers rather than only one.

This kind of information is so important for reservoir engineering purposes that in 
nearly every well drilled in the North Sea a distributed pressure survey is made.
Thus the objective of reservoir monitoring in the early stage of field development can 
be stated succinctly as the identification of the effective permeability of horizontal 
barriers (tight zones such as micaceous streaks, shale layers, stylolites, dolomite 
streaks etc.) and vertical barriers (sealing or partially communicating faults) by 
history matching a reservoir simulator to distributed pressure and flow measurements.
